input.content: Pattern: "Simplification" commits that delete a conditional guard can silently change behavior when the guard was load-bearing. Concrete case (cleanup.py / setup.py): store.active is keyed by workspace_id with value {setup_id, connection} — at most one active setup per workspace. cleanup_setup(store, workspace_id, setup_id) originally popped active[workspace_id] ONLY when active[workspace_id]["setup_id"] == setup_id. A refactor replaced that with an unconditional store.active.pop(workspace_id, None). Regression: cleaning up a superseded/failed setup now evicts the DIFFERENT setup's live active connection for the same workspace. Detection cue: when a value dict stores an identifier (setup_id) precisely to disambiguate which entry owns a slot, an unconditional delete keyed only by the slot (workspace_id) ignores ownership. Existing test only covered the matching-id case, so green tests did not catch it. Reviewer lesson: treat any removed `if ... == id` guard around a pop/delete as a candidate ownership-check regression; construct the cross-id scenario explicitly.
